title: Master Gorbeau
summary: Hugo describes the Gorbeau house, a dilapidated building numbered 50–52 on the Boulevard de l'Hôpital at the bleak southern edge of Paris, and explains how it got its name.
details: The narrator leads the reader to a desolate quarter near the Salpêtrière and the Barrière d'Italie, a place that is neither city nor country, where grass grows in the ruts of the streets. At the corner of the Rue des Vignes-Saint-Marcel stands a low building that looks like a hovel from the road but is in fact enormous: only a door and one large window face the street. The door opens straight onto a steep, ladder-like staircase; the window, once handsome, is patched with paper and broken blinds. Upstairs, a long corridor gives onto a row of cheerless rooms more like stalls than chambers.

The postmen call it Number 50–52; the neighbourhood calls it the Gorbeau house. Hugo tells the anecdote behind the name: around 1770 two Châtelet attorneys named Corbeau (Raven) and Renard (Fox) were so mocked with La Fontaine parodies that they petitioned Louis XV to change their names. The king, in a jovial mood, let Corbeau become Gorbeau and Renard become Prenard. This Maître Gorbeau is said to have owned the building and installed its grand window.

The chapter closes on the gloomy surroundings in 1823: the city wall and its barrier close by, the road to Bicêtre along which the condemned returned to Paris, the elms of the Barrière Saint-Jacques hiding the scaffold, the Salpêtrière on one side and Bicêtre on the other. Hugo reflects on the oppressive symmetry of the place, its sinister aspect at night, and how the Orleans railway has since begun to transform the whole faubourg.

title: A Nest for Owl and a Warbler
summary: Jean Valjean brings the sleeping Cosette into a prepared attic in the Gorbeau house; she wakes the next morning expecting to be set to work and instead is told to play.
details: It is before the Gorbeau house that Jean Valjean stops with Cosette in his arms. He lets himself in with a passkey, climbs the stairs, and opens a modestly furnished attic with a mattress, a table, chairs and a lit stove, with a small dressing-room and folding bed at the far end. He lays the child down without waking her, lights a candle and gazes at her face with a tenderness that is almost ecstasy. He kisses her hand, as nine months earlier he had kissed the hand of her sleeping mother, and kneels by her bed.

In broad daylight a passing cart shakes the building and Cosette starts awake crying 'Yes, madame, here I am!' and gropes for her broom. Then she sees Jean Valjean smiling at her and says, 'Ah, so it is true! Good morning, Monsieur.' She finds her doll Catherine at the foot of the bed and pours out questions: where is she, is Paris big, is Madame Thénardier far away, must she go back? She declares the frightful hole pretty, because she feels free. When she asks whether she must sweep, he tells her to play, and the day passes in happiness.

title: Two Misfortunes Make One Piece of Good Fortune
summary: Jean Valjean, who has never loved anyone, discovers fatherly love for Cosette, and she, who has never been loved, learns to love him; the two settle into a quiet, happy life in the Gorbeau attic.
details: Hugo pauses on what has happened inside Jean Valjean. In fifty-five years he has never been father, lover, husband or friend; his sister and her children are a faded memory. Now all the affection dammed up in him rushes toward this child, and he feels something like a mother's pangs without knowing what they are. After the Bishop, who brought the dawn of virtue, Cosette brings the dawn of love. Cosette, for her part, had a cold heart at eight because no one had let her love anything; from the first day her whole being attaches itself to this kind man, whom she finds handsome just as she finds the hovel pretty. The widower and the orphan, Hugo says, complete each other.

The refuge is well chosen. Their room has the only window in the house, so no neighbour can see in; the ground floor is a wagon-shed with no connection to the upper storey; the only other inhabitant is the old woman who calls herself the 'principal lodger' and acts as portress. Valjean had rented from her on Christmas Eve, presenting himself as a gentleman ruined by Spanish bonds who was coming to live with his little daughter, paying six months in advance and having her furnish the room.

Weeks pass. Cosette sings from daybreak; she is no longer in rags but in mourning. Valjean teaches her to read, remembering that he learned to read in prison with evil intentions, and that this skill now ends in teaching a child. He talks to her of her mother and makes her pray; she calls him 'father' and knows no other name for him. Hugo suggests that Valjean, embittered by Fantine's fate and Javert's authority and sent back to prison for doing right, may have needed this love to persevere in virtue: he is her support, and she is his prop.

title: The Remarks of the Principal Tenant
summary: Valjean goes out only after dark and becomes known as 'the beggar who gives alms'; the inquisitive old portress spies on him, sees him take a thousand-franc note from the lining of his coat, and discovers that his pockets hold wigs and other oddities.
details: Jean Valjean never goes out by day. Each evening at twilight he walks for an hour or two, often with Cosette, keeping to deserted side alleys and visiting churches at nightfall, especially the nearby Saint-Médard. The old woman keeps house and does the marketing; they live soberly. Valjean still wears his yellow coat, black breeches and old hat, and in the street is taken for a poor man; kind women sometimes turn back to give him a sou, which he accepts with a bow. When he meets a beggar he looks about, slips him a coin, often silver, and hurries off. The neighbourhood begins to call him 'the beggar who gives alms.'

The old 'principal lodger,' a cross, slightly deaf and therefore talkative woman with two remaining teeth, watches him closely. She has questioned Cosette, who knows only that she came from Montfermeil. One morning she follows Valjean into an empty room and, through a crack in the door, sees him rip open the lining of his coat and take out a thousand-franc note. He then asks her to go and change it, calling it his quarterly income; she wonders where he could have received it, since he only goes out at six and the bank is shut by then. Her tale of the note sets the gossips of the Rue des Vignes-Saint-Marcel talking.

A few days later, while Valjean saws wood in the corridor, she examines the coat hanging on a nail. The lining has been sewn up, but she feels thicknesses of paper in the skirts and lapels, and the pockets hold needles and thread, a big pocketbook, a very large knife and several wigs of different colours. The chapter ends as winter draws to a close.

title: A Five-Franc Piece Falls on the Ground and Produces a Tumult
summary: Valjean thinks he glimpses Javert's face under a beggar's rags; days later a tall new lodger listens at his door by night, and when Valjean sees his back at dawn he recognises Javert. He gathers his money and leaves with Cosette at nightfall.
details: Near Saint-Médard an old ex-beadle of seventy-five, who crouches by a condemned well mumbling prayers, is one of Valjean's regular beneficiaries; some say he belongs to the police. One evening, as Valjean gives him his alms, the beggar looks up sharply under the newly lit street lamp and drops his head again. In that flash Valjean thinks he has seen not the placid old beadle but a well-known and terrible face. He goes home shaken, hardly daring to admit that the face he thought he saw was Javert's. The next evening he goes back, speaks to the man, and finds the ordinary ex-beadle; he laughs at himself and thinks no more of it.

A few days afterwards, around eight in the evening, while Cosette spells aloud, Valjean hears the house door open and a heavy step come up the stairs, though the old woman always goes to bed at dark. He blows out the candle, sends Cosette softly to bed, and sits motionless. After a while he sees a light through the keyhole: someone with a candle is listening at his door. The light retreats without the sound of footsteps, as if the listener had removed his shoes. Valjean lies awake all night.

At daybreak a door creaks at the end of the corridor and the same step passes his room. Through the keyhole he sees only a tall man in a long frock-coat with a cudgel under his arm, but when the figure is silhouetted at the top of the stairs Valjean has a complete view of his back: the formidable neck and shoulders belong to Javert. When the old woman comes at seven she mentions that a new lodger, 'Dumont, or Daumont,' came in last night, 'a gentleman of property, like yourself.' Valjean rolls up a hundred francs; a five-franc piece slips from his hands and rolls noisily across the floor. At dark he scans the empty boulevard, goes back up, says 'Come' to Cosette, and the two go out.

title: The Zigzags of Strategy
summary: After a note on describing a vanished Paris, Hugo follows Valjean and Cosette through the labyrinth of the Mouffetard quarter by moonlight; from a doorway Valjean watches four men confer in the Rue des Postes and recognises Javert at their head.
details: The author first begs leave to speak of the Paris of his youth in the present tense: he has been long absent, the city has been rebuilt, and he will describe streets and houses as he remembers them even if they no longer stand.

Jean Valjean leaves the boulevard at once and plunges into the side streets, doubling back on his track like a hunted stag. The moon is full; he keeps to the dark side of the streets and watches the light side. Cosette walks on without a question; her early sufferings have made her passive, and she feels safe with him. Valjean has no plan beyond never returning to the Gorbeau house. He is not even certain the man was Javert, or that Javert, if it was he, knows him under his disguise and believes him dead. He winds through the Rue Censier, the Rue Copeau and the lanes near Saint-Victor without entering any lodging house.

As eleven strikes he passes the police commissary's office at 14 Rue de Pontoise and, turning instinctively, sees three men pass under the commissary's lantern close behind him; one goes into the alley to the commissary's house. He hurries Cosette into the Passage des Patriarches and down to the Rue des Postes, where the streets form an open, moonlit square. He hides in a doorway to see whether he is followed. Within three minutes four tall men in long brown coats and round hats, with heavy cudgels, appear and stop to consult. Their leader points in the direction Valjean has taken; as he turns, the moon falls on his face, and Valjean recognises Javert.

title: It Is Lucky That the Pont d’Austerlitz Bears Carriages
summary: Valjean slips away toward the Jardin des Plantes and crosses the Pont d'Austerlitz in the shadow of a cart, but as he enters a dark lane on the far bank he looks back and sees four shadows stepping onto the bridge.
details: While the men hesitate, Valjean leaves his hiding place and goes down the Rue des Postes toward the Jardin des Plantes, carrying the tired Cosette. The street lamps are unlit because of the moon. He passes the Goblet potteries, the Rue de la Clef and the Fountain Saint-Victor, skirts the Jardin des Plantes and reaches the deserted quay. No one is behind him.

At the Pont d'Austerlitz, where tolls are still collected, he offers one sou and the old soldier in charge demands two, since the child he carries can walk. Vexed at having drawn attention, he pays and crosses in the shadow of a heavy cart going the same way. Halfway over Cosette, her feet numb, asks to walk, and he takes her hand. On the right bank he heads for some timber-yards, crossing an open, lit space without hesitation, believing himself hunted but no longer followed.

Before entering the narrow Rue du Chemin-Vert-Saint-Antoine between the timber-yards, he glances back and sees four shadows just stepping onto the bridge from the Jardin des Plantes side. He shudders like a recaptured animal. His one hope is that they did not see him cross the lit ground with Cosette; he commits himself to the dark little street.

title: To Wit, the Plan of Paris in 1727
summary: Valjean takes the right-hand fork toward open country, glimpses movement behind him, and finds himself in the Petit-Picpus quarter with a blind alley on one side and a motionless sentinel barring the other exit; Hugo describes the lost quarter from the 1727 plan.
details: Three hundred paces on, the street forks like a Y. Valjean takes the right branch because it leads toward deserted ground rather than the inhabited suburb. He carries Cosette again, looking back from time to time. At last he sees something moving far behind him in the dark and hurries on, looking for a side street, until he reaches a wall bordering a cross-lane. To the right the lane ends in a blind alley closed by a high white wall; to the left it runs two hundred paces to an open street. As he turns toward the left he sees a man, like a black statue, posted at the corner, barring the way and waiting.

Hugo explains where Valjean is: between the Faubourg Saint-Antoine and La Râpée, a district since rebuilt out of recognition, which old Paris called Le Petit-Picpus. It barely existed as a quarter, more like a monkish Spanish town of walls, gardens, convents and timber-yards, and survives only on the plan of 1727. The Rue du Chemin-Vert-Saint-Antoine splits into the Rue Petit-Picpus on the left and the Rue Polonceau on the right, joined at the top by the Rue Droit-Mur; a dead-end stub of the Rue Droit-Mur is the Cul-de-Sac Genrot.

Valjean stands at the end of the Rue Polonceau. The moving thing he saw behind him must be Javert and his squad; Javert evidently knows this little labyrinth and has sent a man ahead to guard the one exit into the Rue Petit-Picpus. The blind alley cuts him off on one side, the sentinel on the other; to advance is to fall into that man's hands, to retreat is to walk into Javert's arms. Caught as in a slowly tightening net, he looks up at the sky in despair.

title: The Gropings of Flight
summary: Hidden in a niche of the wall, Valjean examines the sombre building at the angle of the Rue Droit-Mur and the Rue Polonceau: the drainpipe will not bear climbing, the carriage gate cannot be forced, and the huge rotten door turns out to be mere boarding over solid stone.
details: Hugo lays out the geography exactly. On the left of the Rue Droit-Mur stands a severe building that rises toward the Rue Petit-Picpus and sinks to a bare wall at the Rue Polonceau corner, where a deep niche hides anyone inside it from observers in either street. The niche is filled by what looks like a colossal, wretched door of planks bound with iron, with an ordinary carriage gate beside it; a linden shows above the wall, and ivy covers it on the Polonceau side.

The building's silent, uninhabited look tempts Valjean. He sets Cosette against a stone post with orders to keep quiet and runs to the lead cistern pipes that branch across the front like a leafless vine, hoping to climb. But the pipe is rotten and barely attached, every window is barred even in the roof, the moon lights the whole façade in view of the sentinel, and in any case he could not haul Cosette up three storeys.

He crawls back to the niche, where he realises he cannot be seen, and tries the doors. The carriage gate is immovable inside and out. The great decrepit door with its three rusted bands looks easy to pierce, but it has no hinges, lock or crossbar: through the gaps he sees rough stone blocks cemented together. It is not a door at all but a wooden facing on a wall.

title: Which Would Be Impossible with Gas Lanterns
summary: With Javert and a platoon of soldiers searching their way up the Rue Polonceau, Valjean cuts down the rope of a street lantern, ties Cosette to it, scales the wall by sheer strength, hauls her up after him, and drops with her into a garden as Javert orders the blind alley searched.
details: A measured tread announces seven or eight soldiers with bayonets coming up the Rue Polonceau, Javert's tall figure at their head and his two agents in the ranks: a patrol he has met and requisitioned. They halt often to search every doorway; at that pace they will reach Valjean in a quarter of an hour. For the third time the galleys yawn before him, and now the galleys mean Cosette lost forever.

Hugo recalls that Valjean, thanks to his escapes from Toulon, is a master of climbing the inner angle of two walls without ladder or irons, using back, shoulders, hips and knees. The wall is about eighteen feet high, with a five-foot mass of masonry filling the corner, so only fourteen feet remain. But he cannot carry Cosette up, and he has no rope. His eye falls on the lantern post in the Cul-de-Sac Genrot: in those days the lanterns were raised and lowered on a rope kept in a locked iron box. In one bound he crosses, forces the box with his knife, and returns with the rope. Since the lanterns are unlit tonight, no one will notice it is gone.

Cosette, frightened by his strange movements and the approaching patrol, whispers that she is afraid and asks who is coming. 'Hush,' he says, 'it is Madame Thénardier,' and warns her that if she cries out the Thénardier will take her back. He passes his cravat under her arms, knots it to the rope, takes the other end in his teeth, throws his shoes and stockings over the wall, and climbs the angle as steadily as a ladder; in half a minute he kneels on top. He tells her to put her back to the wall, lifts her up, puts her on his back and crawls along the crest to where a low roof slopes down to the linden tree inside.

As he reaches the slope, the patrol arrives below with a roar and Javert's voice thunders: search the blind alley, the Rue Droit-Mur and Rue Petit-Picpus are guarded, he is certainly in the alley. The soldiers rush into the Genrot alley. Valjean slides down the roof, reaches the linden, and leaps to the ground with Cosette, who has not made a sound.

title: The Beginning of an Enigma
summary: In a vast, melancholy garden overlooked by barred, lightless façades, Valjean and Cosette hide in a ruined shed while the patrol searches the streets outside; then a hymn of women's voices rises from the dark building, and both fall to their knees.
details: The garden is oblong and strange: an alley of tall poplars at the far end, forest trees in the corners, a great solitary tree in the middle, gnarled fruit trees, vegetable beds, a melon patch whose glass frames glitter in the moonlight, an old well, and stone benches black with moss. Beside Valjean is the ruinous building whose roof brought him down, a pile of fagots, and a mutilated stone statue against the wall. The large building on the Rue Droit-Mur turns two grim façades toward the garden, every window grated, not a gleam of light anywhere. The place seems made for no one to walk in, even by day.

Valjean recovers his shoes and takes Cosette under the shed. She presses against him, trembling, her mind still on the Thénardier. They hear the patrol searching the alley and streets, gunstocks striking the stones, Javert calling to the spies he has posted. After a quarter of an hour the uproar grows distant; Valjean, his hand lightly over Cosette's mouth, holds his breath. Yet the calm within these walls is so profound that the din outside hardly troubles him.

Then a new sound rises out of the gloom: a hymn sung by women's voices, pure as virgins and innocent as children, coming from the dark edifice above the garden. As the noise of the pursuit recedes, it is as though a choir of angels approaches. Cosette and Jean Valjean, not knowing what it is or where they are, kneel. The building still seems deserted; it is a supernatural chant in an uninhabited house. While it lasts Valjean sees not the night but a blue sky. When the song dies away, street and garden are silent, and only dry weeds rustle on the wall.

title: Continuation of the Enigma
summary: Cosette is cold and asks whether Madame Thénardier is still there; Valjean wraps her in his coat and goes looking for better shelter, but through a lit window he sees a shrouded form lying face down on the floor with its arms outstretched and what looks like a rope around its neck, and flees in terror.
details: The night wind has risen; it is between one and two in the morning. Cosette's eyes are wide open and she is still trembling. She says she is very cold, then asks, 'Is she still there?' Valjean has forgotten the fiction he used to silence her, then understands and tells her Madame Thénardier is gone and she need fear nothing more. He takes off his coat and wraps it round her, tells her to wait, and sets out along the great building to find a warmer place.

The doors are locked and the ground-floor windows barred. Round the inner angle he comes to arched windows with a light inside and, on tiptoe, looks into a large flagged hall of pillars and arcades lit by a single taper. On the floor, something covered in a winding-sheet and shaped like a human form lies face down, arms stretched out in a cross, utterly still, with what seems a rope trailing from its neck like a serpent. Valjean, who would say afterward that he had never seen anything more bloodcurdling, presses his face to the glass and watches for a long time; the form never moves.

Seized by terror, he runs back to the shed without daring to look behind him, knees failing and sweat pouring. What is this house, with a street number, that calls souls with the voice of angels and then shows them the gates of the tomb? He touches the stones to be sure it is not a dream. Cold, anxiety and the night's emotions have given him a fever. He goes to Cosette: she is asleep.

title: The Enigma Becomes Doubly Mysterious
summary: A limping figure with a bell moves about the melon beds; Valjean hides Cosette, then finds her hands icy and her breathing faint, and realises she must be in a bed by a fire within a quarter of an hour.
details: Sitting beside the sleeping child, Valjean grows calm and sees the truth that will govern his life henceforth: as long as she is with him he needs nothing and fears nothing except for her. He does not notice that he is cold without his coat.

A faint tinkling, like cattle bells in a night pasture, makes him turn. Someone resembling a man is walking among the bell-glasses of the melon beds, rising and stooping with regular movements as if spreading something on the ground, and he seems to limp. The sound of the bell follows every movement: it approaches when he approaches and ceases when he halts. Who is this man belled like a ram or an ox? Valjean's chimerical fears give way to real ones. Javert's men may still be watching the street; if this gardener finds him he may shout for help. He carries Cosette behind a heap of old furniture in the farthest corner of the shed.

Then he touches Cosette's hands and finds them icy. He calls her name; she does not open her eyes. He shakes her; she does not wake. He fears she is dead. She still breathes, but weakly, and he remembers that sleeping outdoors on a cold night can kill. Everything else vanishes from his mind. He rushes out of the ruin: Cosette must be in bed beside a fire in less than a quarter of an hour.

title: The Man with the Bell
summary: Valjean offers the belled man a hundred francs for a night's shelter and is greeted as 'Father Madeleine': the gardener is old Fauchelevent, whom he once saved from under a cart and placed here. The house is the Petit-Picpus convent. Fauchelevent agrees to ask no questions and takes them into his hidden hut.
details: Valjean walks straight up to the man with the roll of silver in his hand and cries, 'One hundred francs!' if he will give him shelter for the night. The man starts, looks at him in the moonlight, and exclaims, 'What! so it is you, Father Madeleine!' Valjean recoils; he expected anything but that. The speaker is a bent, lame old man dressed like a peasant, with a leather kneecap on his left knee from which hangs a bell. He pours out astonished questions: how did Father Madeleine get in here, without hat, cravat or coat? He says he is the person for whom Valjean got the place here, and that Valjean saved his life. When a ray of moonlight catches his profile, Valjean recognises old Fauchelevent.

Fauchelevent explains that he is covering his melons with straw mats against the frost, which accounts for the movements Valjean watched. The bell on his knee is so that he may be avoided: there are only women and young girls in this house, and when he comes they go. The house is the Petit-Picpus convent, the very one in the Saint-Antoine quarter where, two years before, Fauchelevent was admitted as gardener on the recommendation of the mayor of M. sur M. after his cart crushed him. Fauchelevent insists no man may enter here; Valjean replies that he must stay.

Valjean reminds him gravely: 'Father Fauchelevent, I saved your life.' The old man, trembling with joy, takes his hands and tells Monsieur le Maire to dispose of him. He has an isolated three-room hut behind the ruins of the old convent, in a corner no one looks into. Valjean asks two things: tell no one what you know about me, and do not try to learn more. Fauchelevent agrees, saying Valjean can do nothing dishonest. 'So there is a child?' he says when Valjean mentions her, and asks nothing further.

Within half an hour Cosette is asleep and rosy again in the gardener's bed before a good fire. Valjean has his coat and cravat back on and his hat has been found. The two men warm themselves over bread, cheese and wine, Fauchelevent chiding Father Madeleine for saving people's lives and then forgetting them.

title: Which Explains How Javert Got on the Scent
summary: Hugo tells the pursuit from Javert's side: transferred to Paris, he read of Valjean's death, was stirred by a report of a child abducted at Montfermeil, was put off by Thénardier's 'grandfather' story, then heard of 'the beggar who gives alms,' borrowed the ex-beadle's place, rented a room at the Gorbeau house, and trailed Valjean through Paris, delaying the arrest out of doubt until his quarry vanished.
details: After Valjean escaped from the jail at Montreuil-sur-Mer, the police assumed he had gone to Paris and summoned Javert there to help; his zeal was noticed by M. Chabouillet, secretary of the Prefecture, who had him attached to the Paris police. In December 1823 Javert read in a newspaper that the convict Jean Valjean was dead and thought no more of it. Later a report from the Seine-et-Oise about a child named Cosette, daughter of a Fantine, stolen from an innkeeper at Montfermeil by a stranger, set him thinking: he remembered Valjean asking for three days to fetch that woman's child and being arrested as he boarded the Montfermeil coach. He went to Montfermeil, but Thénardier, wary of drawing the law's eye to his own affairs, had silenced his wife and now described a respectable 'grandfather,' a wealthy farmer called Guillaume Lambert with a passport. Javert returned calling himself a ninny.

In March 1824 he heard of a shy man of means in the parish of Saint-Médard who lived with an eight-year-old girl from Montfermeil, went out only at night, and wore an old yellow coat said to be wadded with banknotes. An old ex-beadle, a police spy who begged near the church, supplied details. To see the man close without alarming him, Javert borrowed the beadle's rags and place for an evening; when the 'suspected individual' gave him alms Javert looked up, and each man recognised, or thought he recognised, the other. But Valjean's death was official and Javert, scrupulous, would not arrest on a doubt. He followed him to the Gorbeau house, got the old woman talking about the thousand-franc note, hired a room and listened at Valjean's door; the next day the old woman, hearing the five-franc piece fall, warned him that the lodger might be leaving, and Javert waited behind the boulevard trees with two men.

Javert had told no one at the Prefecture whose arrest he hoped for: an indiscretion might alert his man, the old hands would take such a prize from a newcomer, and he liked to unveil his masterpieces suddenly. He never lost sight of Valjean, but did not arrest him because he was still in doubt: the fugitive's altered, aged walk, his émigré-tutor costume, Thénardier's grandfather, the official death, and the fear of the newspapers' outcry over an arrested white-haired grandfather all held him back. He also reasoned that if the man was not Valjean he might be some gang chief whose hideouts were worth discovering. Only in the Rue de Pontoise, by the light of a dram-shop, did he positively recognise him; then he asked for reinforcements, which cost him time at the Carrefour Rollin.

Guessing that Valjean would put the river between them, Javert went straight to the Pont d'Austerlitz, learned from the toll-keeper of a man with a little girl, saw him cross the lit ground, remembered the Cul-de-Sac Genrot and the single exit of the Rue Droit-Mur, posted an agent there, requisitioned a passing patrol, and, sure of his prey, took a pinch of snuff and savoured letting him run a little longer. When he closed the net the fly was gone; his sentinel had seen no one pass. Hugo catalogues his blunders: hesitating to recognise, not arresting at the Gorbeau house or in the Rue de Pontoise, consulting in the moonlight, and above all playing cat and mouse. The cut lantern rope led him to search the gardens off the blind alley all night; at daybreak he left two men on watch and returned to the Prefecture ashamed.

title: Number 62 Rue Petit-Picpus
summary: Hugo takes the reader through the carriage gate of 62 Rue Petit-Picpus, up a narrow stair to a bare room with a grated hole, past a password and a portress's voice, into a grated, shuttered parlour where a veiled nun may speak but cannot be seen: this is the Convent of the Bernardines of the Perpetual Adoration.
details: From the street, Number 62 looks like any other carriage gate, usually ajar, showing a vine-hung courtyard and a lounging porter, with tall trees beyond. Yet the house behind the smiling threshold prays and weeps. Past the porter, who admits only those who know the formula, a narrow yellow-and-chocolate staircase and a turning corridor lead to an unfastened door and a small, clean, utterly empty room. In the facing wall is a square hole closed by a black iron grating reinforced with a pierced sheet of tin, with a letter-box slot and a bell-pull beside it.

Pull the tape and a gentle, mournful woman's voice very close by asks who is there. Without the second password the voice falls silent; with it, it says 'Enter on the right.' There, through a glass door, is a narrow box like a grated theatre box, with two old chairs and a black wooden ledge, closed by a monstrous iron lattice and, six inches beyond it, black shutters that are always shut. After a while a voice behind the shutters says, 'I am here. What do you wish with me?' Under rare conditions a slat opens, and behind grating and shutter appears a head of which only mouth and chin can be seen beneath a black veil and guimpe; it speaks but never looks at you or smiles. Behind her the visitor sees only night and emptiness: the interior of a cloister.

This is the Convent of the Bernardines of the Perpetual Adoration; the box is the parlour, the first voice the portress who sits motionless beside the grated opening. The parlour has a window on the world's side and none on the convent's, for profane eyes must see nothing of the sacred place. Yet there is life behind that shadow, and Hugo announces that he will take the reader inside and tell things that storytellers have never described.

title: The Obedience of Martin Verga
summary: Hugo describes the rule of the Bernardines-Benedictines of Martin Verga at the Petit-Picpus: their descent from Cîteaux and Saint Benoît, their black habit, their fasts, scourging, silence and night offices, the twelve-hour 'reparation' with a rope around the neck, the Perpetual Adoration, the chapter of faults, and the parlour through which only the prioress may deal with outsiders.
details: The convent, long established by 1824, belongs to the Bernardines of the obedience of Martin Verga, a Spanish congregation founded in 1425 and attached to Cîteaux, hence to Saint Benoît rather than Saint Bernard. Hugo distinguishes them from the Benedictine Ladies of the Holy Sacrament at the Temple and the Rue Neuve-Sainte-Geneviève, who also practise the Perpetual Adoration but wear a white guimpe and a silver-gilt Holy Sacrament; the Petit-Picpus nuns wear all black except a white band, novices all white.

Theirs is the harshest rule after the barefoot Carmelites: fasting all year and abstaining from meat, rising between one and three to chant matins, sleeping on straw between serge sheets, never bathing or lighting a fire, scourging themselves every Friday, keeping silence except in brief recreations, and wearing a fever-inducing drugget chemise from September 14 to Easter. The prioress is elected for three years and may serve at most nine. They never see the priest, hidden by a nine-foot serge curtain; only the archbishop may enter, and the old gardener, who wears a bell on his knee so that they may avoid him. Submission to the prioress is absolute; they may not read or write without leave.

Each in turn makes 'reparation': twelve hours kneeling on stone before the Holy Sacrament with hands clasped and a rope around her neck, lying prostrate in a cross when exhausted, praying for all the sins of the world. Because it is done before a post with a candle, they call it 'being at the post.' Another sister is always kneeling before the Holy Sacrament in hourly relays: the Perpetual Adoration. Mothers bear names such as Nativity or Passion. They never say 'my,' only 'our'; cells stay open; greetings and knocks are answered with 'Forever'; at every hour three bell strokes stop all speech for the formula praising the Holy Sacrament. They chant in full voice, and for the office of the dead in a tone almost too low for women.

They have a burial vault under the altar but the government forbids its use; they may be buried at a special hour in a corner of the old Vaugirard cemetery. A weekly chapter hears each sister confess her faults aloud; lesser offences bring the self-imposed coulpe, lying prostrate before the prioress until she taps her stall. Nuns summoned to the parlour drop their veils; only the prioress may communicate with strangers, others see family rarely and through the shutters, and men are always refused. These nuns are pale and grave; between 1825 and 1830 three of them went mad.

title: Austerities
summary: Hugo describes the years of postulancy and novitiate, the profession ceremony in which the novice is covered with a black veil while the office of the dead is sung, and the boarding-school of noble girls attached to the convent, who see even their mothers only through the parlour bars.
details: A postulant waits two to four years, a novice four; final vows seldom come before twenty-three or twenty-four, and widows are not admitted. In their cells the nuns practise unspoken macerations. On the day of her profession the novice is dressed in her finest clothes and crowned with white roses, then prostrates herself; a great black veil is thrown over her and the office for the dead is sung. The nuns pass in two files, one lamenting 'Our sister is dead,' the other answering 'Our sister is alive in Jesus Christ.'

At the time of the story a boarding-school for girls of noble, mostly wealthy families is attached to the convent, with pupils such as the Mesdemoiselles de Saint-Aulaire and de Bélissen and an English Talbot. Reared between four walls, they grow up with a horror of the world; one told Hugo that the sight of street pavement made her shudder. They wear blue with a white cap and a Holy Spirit on the breast, and on great feasts such as Saint Martha's day they are allowed, as a supreme treat, to dress as nuns and keep the full offices for a day, an amusement the convent encourages.

The pupils follow all the practices except the austerities, and some keep the reflex of answering 'Forever' long after marriage. Like the nuns they see relatives only in the parlour; even mothers cannot embrace them. Hugo recounts a girl who wept to kiss her three-year-old sister and begged that the child's hand at least be passed through the bars, which was almost indignantly refused.

title: Gayeties
summary: The pupils fill the gloomy cloister with childhood: recreation hours in the garden, and a string of children's sayings Hugo collected there, from the little girl who rejoices at having only nine years and ten months left to the foundling who murmurs that her mother was not there when she was born.
details: At the recreation hour a door swings open and youth floods the garden cut by a cross-shaped path; after the psalms and knells the girls' voices burst out sweeter than bees, and the veiled nuns watch the laughter from a distance. Hugo says Homer would have come there to laugh with Perrault. The nuns are gentle with the children, severe only toward themselves.

He records sayings from those walls: a five-year-old delighted to learn she has 'only nine years and ten months longer to remain here'; a quarrel in which little Alix opened the history book at random and asked 'What happened after that?'; a remark on a well-bred parakeet that eats the top of its bread and butter like a person; a seven-year-old's written confession accusing herself of avarice, adultery and raising her eyes to the gentlemen; a six-year-old's tale of three little cocks eaten by a wolf; a rhyme about Punchinello and the cat; and a foundling raised by the convent out of charity who, hearing the others talk of their mothers, says that hers was not there when she was born.

The stout portress with her keys, Sister Agatha, is nicknamed Agathocles by the big girls. The dark, damp refectory is 'full of beasts,' and its four corners are named Spider, Caterpillar, Woodlouse and Cricket; each pupil belongs to the 'nation' of her corner, so that when the Archbishop visits and asks who a pretty girl is, he is told 'She is a spider, Monseigneur,' and his informant declares herself a woodlouse. Hugo adds a parallel from Écouen, where girls were ranked as 'virgins' and 'florists' for the procession, and a seven-year-old told a sixteen-year-old, 'You are a virgin, but I am not.'

title: Distractions
summary: More of the convent's inner life: the 'white Paternoster' over the refectory door, the silent meals and the punishment of licking the pavement, the pupils' stolen fruit and forbidden reading of the rule, Mademoiselle Bouchard's wager with the Archbishop, the mysterious mad Madame Albertine who cries 'Ah! Auguste!' at the Duc de Rohan's sermon, and the flute from the Rue Droit-Mur that turned out to be a blind old émigré.
details: Above the refectory door was painted the 'white Paternoster,' a folk prayer promising paradise to whoever recites it thrice at evening and morning; by 1827 it was painted over. The pupils ate in silence at black tables under white walls, a single dish of meat and vegetables or salt fish, while a big girl read lives of the saints from a little pulpit and the supervising mother snapped a wooden book at any noise. A child who broke silence 'made a cross with her tongue' by licking the floor. The pupils once got hold of the forbidden rule of Saint-Benoît and found it dull except for some unintelligible pages about the sins of young boys; they hid windfall apples and pears under their pillows and ate them in bed, as a letter from a former pupil, now a duchess, attests.

During an archiepiscopal visit Mademoiselle Bouchard, a Montmorency connection, bet that she would ask for a day's leave, an enormity there. She stepped from the ranks and asked; M. de Quélen smiled and granted three days, and the prioress could do nothing. Hugo also records, as a fact unconnected with his story, the mysterious Madame Albertine: not a nun, treated with great respect, said to be mad and to 'pass for dead' in the world, where her supposed death served some great marriage settlement. Pale, cold to the touch, gliding rather than walking, she alone heard the offices from the Œil-de-Bœuf gallery, from which the priest could be seen. When the young Duc de Rohan preached for the first time she half rose and cried, 'Ah! Auguste!' then sank back into immobility; the convent buzzed, since Auguste was indeed his name and she had used it as a pet name.

The schoolgirls, who could not see M. de Rohan, a former musketeer and now vicar-general, knew his sweet, shrill voice and dreamed of his well-dressed hair and elegant cassock. Two severe duchesses, Mesdames de Choiseul and de Sérent, terrified them when they visited. One year a flute began to play 'My Zétulbé, come reign o'er my soul' from the Rue Droit-Mur two or three times a day for months; the girls fell in love with the unknown musician, punishments rained, one waved a handkerchief through a grating, and two climbed onto a roof at the risk of their lives to see him. He was an old, blind, penniless émigré gentleman playing in his attic to pass the time.

title: The Little Convent
summary: The enclosure holds three buildings: the Great Convent, the Boarding-school, and the Little Convent, a refuge for aged nuns of orders destroyed by the Revolution and a few old society ladies, including briefly Madame de Genlis. Hugo describes the church that divides them, built so no inhabitant of the cloister can see a face from outside.
details: Within the Petit-Picpus are three distinct buildings. Besides the Great Convent of the nuns and the Boarding-school of the pupils stands the Little Convent, with its own garden, where old nuns of every order, relics of cloisters destroyed in the Revolution, live under the Empire's permission and a small pension, each keeping her own rule: a 'harlequin convent' of black, grey and white habits. The pupils sometimes visited them as a treat and remembered Mothers Sainte-Bazile, Sainte-Scolastique and Jacob. One refugee, the last nun of Sainte-Aure, whose order once occupied this very house, was too poor to wear her white robe and scarlet scapular and dressed a little manikin in it instead; the doll outlived the order.

Some old society women also retired there with the prioress's leave, like Madame Albertine, Madame Beaufort d'Hautpoul and the Marquise Dufresne, and one known to the pupils only as Madame Vacarmini for the noise she made blowing her nose. Around 1820 Madame de Genlis, then editing a little periodical, asked to enter as a lady resident on the Duc d'Orléans's recommendation; the vocal mothers fluttered because she had written novels, but she declared she detested them and got in. She left after six or eight months complaining that the garden had no shade, to the nuns' delight, leaving pasted in her cupboard five lines of sixth-century Latin verse about the two thieves of Calvary, which she believed kept robbers away.

The church separates the Great Convent from the Boarding-school like an entrenchment and is common to all three houses; the public may enter by a sort of lazaretto door on the street. But the choir is folded back into a dark hall at the priest's right, shut off by a seven-foot curtain, with the nuns on the left, the schoolgirls on the right and the lay-sisters and novices behind; the public knows they are present only by the clatter of the folding stall seats.

title: Some Silhouettes of This Darkness
summary: Hugo names the convent's people in 1819–1825: the learned, merry prioress Mademoiselle de Blemeur, Mother Innocente; the nearly blind sub-prioress Mother Cineres; the vocal mothers and lay-sisters; the bell code by which the silent house communicates; and the two men besides archbishop and gardener whom the pupils ever see, an old ugly chaplain and a hunchbacked drawing-master.
details: From 1819 to 1825 the prioress was Mademoiselle de Blemeur, Mother Innocente in religion, of the family of the author of the Lives of the Saints of the Order of Saint-Benoît. About sixty, short and thick, 'singing like a cracked pot,' she was an excellent woman and the only merry one in the convent, and adored for it; learned in history, Latin, Greek and Hebrew, she was more Benedictine monk than Benedictine nun, and had been re-elected. The sub-prioress was Mother Cineres, an old Spanish nun almost blind.

Hugo lists the vocal mothers: Sainte-Honorine the treasurer, Sainte-Gertrude mistress of novices, Saint-Ange her assistant, Annonciation the sacristan, Saint-Augustin the nurse and the only malicious one, the young and beautiful-voiced Sainte-Mechtilde who drilled seven pupils of graduated ages into a 'living pan-pipe of angels,' and others with their worldly names, two of whom went mad; also the pretty twenty-three-year-old Mother Assumption from the Isle de Bourbon. The lay-sisters the pupils loved most were Euphrasie, Sainte-Marguerite, the doting Sainte-Marthe and long-nosed Sainte-Michel. All were gentle with the children, who alone had fire and better food, though a nun addressed by a child never replied.

Because speech was withdrawn from people, it passed to things: the church bell and the gardener's bell spoke, and a sonorous bell by the portress rang a code for every person and action, one-and-one for the prioress, six-five for lessons, four-four for Madame de Genlis, nine strokes for the opening of the iron 'door of seclusion' only when the archbishop came. Besides archbishop and gardener the schoolgirls saw two other men: the chaplain Abbé Banés, old and ugly, glimpsed through a grating, and the drawing-master M. Ansiaux, 'a frightful old hunchback.' All these men, Hugo notes, were carefully chosen.

title: Post Corda Lapides
summary: Hugo sketches the physical plan of the convent: a trapezium bounded by the Rue Polonceau, Rue Droit-Mur, Rue Petit-Picpus and the Aumarais lane, its buildings laid out like a flattened gibbet, its sunken garden radiating alleys from a central fir, built on the site of a medieval tennis-court called 'the eleven thousand devils.'
details: After the convent's moral face, its material configuration. The convent fills nearly the whole trapezium between four streets that ring it like a moat. Seen from above, the main building traces a gibbet laid flat: the long arm along the Rue Droit-Mur holds the cells of mothers, sisters and novices; the shorter arm, a grey grated façade on the Rue Petit-Picpus ending at the carriage entrance Number 62, holds kitchens, refectory, cloisters and church, with a low dusty arched door that is the public entrance to the church, opened only on Sundays and when a nun's coffin leaves. The elbow is the servants' hall the nuns call 'the buttery.' The school, invisible from the street, lies between Number 62 and the closed Aumarais lane.

The rest is the garden, sunk well below the Rue Polonceau so that the walls are far higher inside than out. From a conical fir on a central hillock run four grand alleys and eight small ones, like a cross on a wheel, bordered with currant bushes; an alley of tall poplars links the ruins of the old convent at the Rue Droit-Mur corner to the Little Convent at the Aumarais corner, with its 'little garden.' The whole stands on the site of a famous fourteenth-to-sixteenth-century tennis-ground, 'the tennis-ground of the eleven thousand devils.' The streets are older than Paris: Aumarais was once Maugout lane, and the Rue Droit-Mur the Rue des Églantiers, 'for God opened flowers before man cut stones.'

title: A Century Under a Guimpe
summary: A digression on a centenarian nun from Fontevrault in the Little Convent, who chattered of pre-Revolutionary society and the 'four wines,' and kept a locked treasure no one might see: after her death it proved to be a comic Faenza platter of Cupids chased by apothecary boys with syringes.
details: Hugo begs one more digression to show that the cloister has its original figures. In the Little Convent lived a centenarian from the Abbey of Fontevrault who had been in society before the Revolution and loved to drop the names of M. de Miromesnil, Keeper of the Seals, and a Presidentess Duplat. She spoke with a Picard accent that amused the pupils, said Fontevrault was like a city with streets, and each year, renewing her vows, recited a chain of saints who had passed the oath from one to another before she gave it to the priest, which set the girls laughing under their veils.

She claimed the Bernardine monks of her youth were as good as the musketeers, and described the old custom of the four wines, in which a great lord passing through Burgundy or Champagne was offered four goblets labelled monkey, lion, sheep and hog wine, the four stages of drunkenness. In a locked cupboard she kept a mysterious object she showed to no one, shutting herself up to contemplate it and falling silent whenever it was mentioned, which set the whole idle convent guessing at relics and holy books.

When she died they rushed to the cupboard and found, under a triple linen cloth, a Faenza platter painted with little Loves fleeing apothecary lads armed with enormous syringes, one Cupid already spitted: 'Love conquered by the colic.' The platter was still for sale on the Boulevard Beaumarchais in 1845. The old woman refused all visitors from outside because, she said, 'the parlour is too gloomy.'

title: Origin of the Perpetual Adoration
summary: Hugo contrasts the Petit-Picpus parlour with the friendlier one at the Temple convent and recounts how the Benedictines of the Perpetual Adoration were founded after sacrileges in two Paris churches in 1649, distinguishing them again from the Bernardines of the Petit-Picpus, who were authorised to practise the same adoration in 1657.
details: The sepulchral parlour just described is a local trait. At the Temple convent, which belonged to another order, brown curtains replaced black shutters and the parlour was a polished salon with muslin curtains, a portrait of an unveiled Benedictine, painted bouquets and even the head of a Turk; its garden held the chestnut tree reputed 'father of all the chestnut trees of the realm.'

The Temple house belonged to the Benedictines of the Perpetual Adoration, an order barely two hundred years old. In 1649 the holy sacrament was profaned at Saint-Sulpice and Saint-Jean-en-Grève; a solemn procession did not satisfy two pious women, Madame Courtin, Marquise de Boucs, and the Comtesse de Châteauvieux, who in 1652 and 1653 endowed Mother Catherine de Bar to found a Benedictine monastery devoted to perpetual adoration, on condition that each entrant bring three hundred livres of income. The Abbé of Saint-Germain, then the king, then the Chamber of Accounts and Parliament in 1654 confirmed it; the first convent was in the Rue Cassette.

That order descends from the Abbé of Saint-Germain des Prés, as the Sacred Heart ladies from the Jesuits and the Sisters of Charity from the Lazarists, and is wholly different from the Cîteaux Bernardines of the Petit-Picpus, whom Pope Alexander VII authorised in 1657 to practise the Perpetual Adoration too. The two orders nonetheless remained distinct.

title: End of the Petit-Picpus
summary: By the Restoration the convent was already in decay; by 1840 the school and the Little Convent were gone and the nuns dwindled from near a hundred to a handful. Hugo explains why he has entered this house in Jean Valjean's story and states his stance: respect without belief, and vigilance against a past that disguises itself as the future.
details: At the start of the Restoration the Petit-Picpus was declining with the whole order, as all religious orders have declined since the eighteenth century. By 1840 the Little Convent and the school had vanished, the old women dead and the girls gone. The rule of Perpetual Adoration is so harsh that vocations recoil from it; in 1845 it still found a few lay-sisters but no professed nuns. Forty years earlier there were nearly a hundred nuns, fifteen years earlier twenty-eight; the burden stays the same for the few as for the many, and it crushes them. In Hugo's own Paris years two died, aged twenty-five and twenty-three. This decay is why the convent gave up educating girls.

Hugo says he could not pass this extraordinary house without entering it and bringing his readers in, for the profit, perhaps, of the melancholy history of Jean Valjean. He has described it in detail but with respect, understanding not everything and insulting nothing, standing between Joseph de Maistre's anointing of the executioner and Voltaire's sneer at the cross. The nineteenth century is unlearning things, and rightly, but there is no vacuum in the human heart and demolitions must be followed by reconstructions.

Meanwhile, he says, let us study what is no more, if only to avoid it: the past counterfeits itself and calls itself the future, wearing the face of superstition and the mask of hypocrisy. Convents pose a complex problem: civilisation condemns them, liberty protects them.

title: The Convent as an Abstract Idea
summary: Opening his 'Parenthesis,' Hugo declares that this book is a drama whose chief personage is the Infinite, and that a convent, like synagogue, mosque, pagoda or wigwam, is one of the instruments man applies to the Infinite, with a hideous side he execrates and a sublime side he adores.
details: Hugo states that this book is a drama whose leading personage is the Infinite, and man the second. A convent having happened to be on the road, it was his duty to enter it, because the convent, common to East and West, to antiquity and modern times, to paganism, Buddhism, Islam and Christianity, is one of the optical apparatuses man applies to the Infinite.

While keeping all his reserves, restrictions and even indignations, he confesses that whenever he meets man in the Infinite, well or ill understood, he is overcome with respect. Every place of worship has a hideous side he execrates and a sublime side he adores; the reverberation of God upon the human wall is endless food for thought.

title: The Convent as an Historical Fact
summary: Judged by history and reason, monasticism stands condemned: good at the dawn of civilisation, it is a parasite on grown nations, and the old Spanish convent in particular was a place of horror. Against those who dismiss such accounts as 'declamation,' Hugo describes the in pace dungeons he saw himself at the Abbey of Villers near Brussels.
details: From the standpoint of history, reason and truth, Hugo condemns monasticism. Monasteries that abound in a nation clog its circulation like mistletoe on an oak; useful when the brutal needed taming by the spiritual, they are detestable in the nineteenth century, and their leprosy has gnawed Italy and Spain nearly to skeletons, from which only 1789 is letting them recover.

The ancient female convent, above all the Spanish one, is for him the point where horrors intersect: huge dark altars, bleeding ivory Christs hung with rubies and diamonds, veiled women bruised by hair shirts and scourges who neither think, will, love nor live, with an abbess who is a spectre. He likens the Spanish convent to an oriental seraglio of souls, the archbishop its keeper, the nun its odalisque, where a glance at the world was infidelity and the in pace replaced the drowning sack.

Defenders of the past now simply smile at such facts and call Rousseau, Diderot, Voltaire and even Tacitus 'declaimers.' Facts are obstinate: Hugo has seen with his own eyes, eight leagues from Brussels at the Abbey of Villers, the hole of the oubliettes and four half-submerged stone dungeons by the river Thil, the in pace, with a rusted iron collar riveted to one wall and a granite box too short to lie in and too low to stand in, closed with a stone lid, where a living being was shut up. This exists, he says; it can be touched. 'What declaimers!'

title: On What Conditions One Can Respect the Past
summary: Monasticism as Spain practised it is a consumption of civilisation, yet the spirit of the cloister persists in the nineteenth century, propped up by theorists who whitewash the past as 'social order.' Hugo will respect the past only if it consents to be dead, and fights it when it insists on living, while refusing to exaggerate.
details: Monasticism of the Spanish or Tibetan kind is a phthisis of civilisation: it depopulates, castrates, forces vocations, feeds feudalism with younger sons, walls up brains and buries living souls. Yet the spirit of the cloister persists, and an ascetic revival is astonishing the civilised world. Hugo mocks the obstinacy of dead institutions with a chorus of the old garment, the stale fish, the faded perfume and the corpse that each plead 'I served you once,' to which the only answer is 'In former days.'

Theorists who would embalm the past relabel it social order, divine right, family, tradition and religion, like the ancient soothsayers who chalked a black heifer white. Hugo will respect and spare the past where it consents to be dead; if it insists on living he attacks it, for humanity is condemned to eternal war with phantoms. A convent in the Paris of '89, 1830 and 1848 is a college of owls facing the light, an anachronism; in ordinary times one need only make it spell out its date.

'Let us fight,' he says, but with distinction: truth never exaggerates, and some things must be destroyed while others need only be examined and elucidated. He opposes ascetic claustration everywhere, in Asia as in Europe, as a marsh and a plague. That said, the religious question remains, with its mysterious and formidable sides, and he asks leave to look at it fixedly.

title: The Convent from the Point of View of Principles
summary: Considered abstractly, the monastery rests on the rights of association and of shutting one's door, and realises equality and fraternity: all share the same cell, bread and straw, titles vanish, and the members elect those they obey. Hugo grants it a deferential gravity when it is wholly voluntary, then asks what these kneeling people in the dark are doing.
details: People unite in communities by the right of association, shut themselves in by the right every man has to open or close his door, and stay in by the right to come and go. Inside, they speak low, drop their eyes, work, renounce the world and own nothing: the rich man becomes poor, the lord equals the peasant, all take the same tonsure and frock, eat the same black bread, sleep on the same straw, bear only first names, dissolve the carnal family into a spiritual one, tend the poor and sick, and elect those they obey, calling each other brother.

To the objection that this is the ideal convent, Hugo answers that it is enough that it is the possible convent. That is why he spoke of the Petit-Picpus with respect. Setting aside the Middle Ages, Asia and the political question, and on condition that the monastery is absolutely voluntary and holds only consenting members, he will always regard a cloistered community with attentive and in some respects deferential gravity. Where there is a community there is a commune and therefore right; the monastery is Equality and Fraternity, and liberty would transform it into a republic.
But what do these men and women behind four walls do besides dressing alike and calling each other brothers? They gaze on the darkness, kneel, and clasp their hands. What does this signify?

title: Prayer
summary: They pray, to God; Hugo asks what that means and answers with his theology of two infinities, one above us and one within, whose contact through thought is prayer. He calls for respecting thought, reverie and prayer, crushing fanaticism while venerating the infinite, and clearing God of caterpillars.
details: They pray, to God. Hugo asks what the words mean. Is there an infinite beyond us, necessarily substantial and intelligent since it is infinite, the absolute of which we are only the relative? And is there not also an infinite within us, superposed on and mirroring the first, an abyss concentric with another abyss? If both infinities are intelligent each has a will and an I: the I below is the soul, the I above is God. To bring the infinity below into contact with the infinity above by means of thought is to pray.

He asks that nothing be taken from the human mind: suppression is bad, reform and transformation are the way. Thought, reverie and prayer are faculties turned toward the Unknown, that ocean whose compass is conscience; they are majestic radiations of the soul into the shadow, which is to say the light. Democracy's grandeur is to deny nothing of humanity, and beside the rights of man stands the right of the soul.

The law is to crush fanaticism and venerate the infinite. Beyond contemplating the starry tree of creation, we must labour over the human soul, defend mystery against miracle, adore the incomprehensible and reject the absurd, purify belief, strip superstition from religion, and 'clear God of caterpillars.'

title: The Absolute Goodness of Prayer
summary: All sincere modes of prayer are good. Hugo attacks the philosophy that denies the infinite as a kind of blindness, argues that denying God leads to nihilism and that nihilism refutes itself, and insists that philosophy must be an energy that improves man's condition, with faith and love as the two motors of progress toward the ideal, which is God.
details: Every sincere mode of prayer is good; 'turn your book upside down and be in the infinite.' A philosophy that denies the infinite is like a philosophy that denies the sun: blindness. Hugo mocks the mole's pity for those with their sun, yet salutes the great atheists as philosophers, saying that by their very force they prove God, while denouncing their philosophy. He dismisses a northern metaphysical school that replaces 'force' with 'will': if the plant wills and so has an I, then the universe wills and so has a God.

To deny the will of the infinite is to deny the infinite, which leads to nihilism, where everything becomes 'a mental conception' and no discussion is possible since the nihilist doubts even his interlocutor; yet by uttering the word 'mind' he admits all he denied. To 'No' the only reply is 'Yes.' There is no nothingness; man lives by affirmation even more than by bread.

Philosophy should be an energy that betters man: Socrates entering Adam to produce Marcus Aurelius, Eden turned into a Lyceum, science as a cordial, wisdom as holy communion, so that philosophy is promoted to religion. Hugo closes by naming the two motors of man's departure and progress's end, faith and love. Progress is the goal, the ideal is the type, and the ideal is God; ideal, absolute, perfection and infinity are identical words.

title: Precautions to Be Observed in Blame
summary: Fighting tyrants and bad lawgivers is simple, but the right to live apart must be reckoned with. The convent is a contradiction, supreme egoism yielding supreme abnegation, a bill drawn on death; one may frown at it but never sneer.
details: History and philosophy have clear duties, to combat Caiaphas, Draco, Trimalchio and Tiberius, but the right to live apart, with all its abuses, insists on being stated and taken into account. Cenobitism is a human problem, and about convents, abodes of error and innocence, aberration and goodwill, torture and martyrdom, one must finally say yes or no.

A convent is a contradiction: its object salvation, its means sacrifice; supreme egoism resulting in supreme abnegation; abdication in order to reign. In the cloister one suffers in order to enjoy, draws a bill of exchange on death, accepts hell in advance as a post-obit on paradise. Taking the veil is a suicide paid for with eternity. Mockery is not permissible on such a subject; everything about it, good and bad, is serious. The just man frowns but never sneers: wrath is understandable, malice is not.

title: Faith, Law
summary: Hugo closes the parenthesis by saluting the man who kneels: to contemplate is to labour, cenobites are not idlers, and there must be some who pray constantly for those who never pray. He is for religion against religions, and, not sharing these women's belief, regards them with a tender and religious terror as souls dwelling on the brink of the mystery.
details: A few words more. Hugo blames the church when it is full of intrigue and despises the spiritual when it is harsh to the temporal, but honours the thoughtful man everywhere and salutes the man who kneels. Faith is a necessity; woe to him who believes nothing. Contemplation is labour and thought is action: folded arms toil, clasped hands work, and Thales, motionless for four years, founded philosophy. A perpetual memory of the tomb is proper for the living, and on this the ascetic and the sage converge.

To those who ask what use these motionless figures are, he answers that there is probably no work more divine or more useful, and that there must be some who pray constantly for those who never pray at all; the whole question is how much thought is mingled with the prayer. Leibnitz praying is grand, Voltaire adoring is fine. He is for religion as against religions, believing in the wretchedness of orisons and the sublimity of prayer, and in an age of low brows and enjoyment-morality he venerates whoever exiles himself. Sacrifice wrongly directed is still sacrifice.

The female convent in particular has a certain majesty, since in this century it is woman who suffers most and her cloistered exile is a kind of protest. This austere existence is neither life, since it is not liberty, nor the tomb, since it is not plenitude, but a misty frontier between two abysses. Hugo, who does not believe what these women believe but lives by faith like them, has never been able to think without tender, religious terror and envious pity of these trembling, trusting souls who dwell on the brink of the mystery, kneeling, bewildered, half lifted by the deep breaths of eternity.

title: Which Treats of the Manner of Entering a Convent
summary: Hugo returns to Valjean in Fauchelevent's hut: the hymn was matins, the hall the chapel, the prostrate form the sister making reparation. Valjean resolves to stay in the convent; Fauchelevent, resolved to save 'M. Madeleine' whatever he is, explains that a nun has just died, that the pupils would discover any man in the garden, and that to be admitted Valjean must first get out and come back in by the door. A fourth peal summons the gardener to the prioress.
details: Into this house Valjean had, as Fauchelevent put it, fallen from the sky. The hymn he heard was the nuns chanting matins; the hall was the chapel; the shrouded form was the sister making reparation; the bell was on Fauchelevent's knee. After their supper the two men lie down on straw, Cosette having the only bed, and neither sleeps. Valjean, knowing Javert is on his scent, sees that he and Cosette are lost if they return to Paris, and that this convent is both the most dangerous place, since a man found there is one step from prison, and the safest, since no one would look for him in an impossible place. His one thought is to remain.

Fauchelevent cudgels his brains: how did M. Madeleine come over such walls, with a child, and who is she? He has heard nothing of Montreuil-sur-Mer since he came here and guesses at bankruptcy or some political trouble, which pleases his old Bonapartism. He does not understand, but one thing is certain: M. Madeleine saved his life, and did not stop to deliberate before crawling under the cart. He resolves to save him whether he is a saint, a thief or an assassin. Hugo adds that Fauchelevent, a Picard peasant, had once been a notary, which added trickery to his cunning; failing in business he became a carter, but kept his grammar and his wit, and the convent's air had made a good deed necessary to him.

At daybreak Fauchelevent asks, 'Now that you are here, how are you going to contrive to enter?' First, neither Valjean nor the child must set foot outside the hut. They have come at an inauspicious moment: one of the ladies is dying, the forty hours' prayers are being said, and the community is absorbed; a bell strikes once, then again: the knell, which will sound once a minute for twenty-four hours. The hidden hut is no refuge, because of the little girls, who chase stray balls everywhere in recreation and would shriek 'a man!'; today there will be no recreation. Valjean notes that there are pupils and thinks that here is Cosette's education provided. 'This convent would be our salvation,' he murmurs; the difficulty is to remain. 'No,' says Fauchelevent, 'the difficulty is to get out,' for the nuns require one to enter by the door, and Valjean cannot possibly return to the street where the police are swarming: 'Say that I fell from the sky.'

Fauchelevent sketches a plan for Cosette: he will carry her out in his vintage basket on his back, past the porter, to a deaf old fruit-seller he knows in the Rue du Chemin-Vert who will keep her overnight as his niece. For Valjean he has no idea; Valjean asks for some way out 'in a basket, under cover, like Cosette.' Further peals mark the doctor of the dead being summoned and departing. Fauchelevent rambles about his duties: he nails up the nuns' coffins in the dead-room off the church, which no man but the doctor may enter, and the undertaker's men take them to the Vaugirard cemetery, where his friend Father Mestienne is gravedigger and the nuns have leave to be buried at nightfall. 'Mother Crucifixion is dead, and Father Madeleine—' 'Is buried,' says Valjean, smiling sadly. A fourth peal summons the gardener; he buckles on his bell, tells Valjean not to stir, and hurries off to the parlour where the prioress is waiting.

title: Fauchelevent in the Presence of a Difficulty
summary: Before the prioress, Mother Innocente, Fauchelevent boldly asks that his 'brother,' an excellent gardener, be allowed to come and help him, bringing a little daughter to be reared in the house. The prioress replies only by asking whether he can procure a stout iron bar by evening, to serve as a lever, and withdraws to the chapter.
details: The prioress, Mademoiselle de Blemeur, Mother Innocente, usually cheerful, wears a grave and agitated air. She calls him 'Father Fauvent,' the convent's abbreviation, and says she has sent for him; he answers, with a boldness that terrifies him inwardly, that he too has a request. Hugo explains Fauchelevent's standing: in more than two years of solitary gardening he has learned to read every peal and clothe the veiled shadows with flesh, and has set the porter and the gravedigger chattering so that he knows the nuns' life and their death. He knows all and conceals all; the convent thinks him stupid, which is a great merit in religion, and the vocal mothers make much of him.

With the assurance of a man who feels appreciated, he launches into a long rustic harangue about his age, his infirmities, the size of the garden and nights like the last spent covering melons, and concludes that he has a brother, no longer young, an excellent gardener, who would come and help him, failing which he himself must regretfully leave; and that the brother has a little daughter who might be reared for God in the house and might one day become a nun. The prioress makes a movement at the word 'brother' and a second, reassured one at 'no longer young.'

When he has finished she stops her rosary and asks whether he can procure a stout iron bar between now and evening. 'For what purpose?' 'To serve as a lever.' He says yes. Without another word she rises and goes into the adjoining chapter hall, where the vocal mothers are probably assembled, leaving Fauchelevent alone.

title: Mother Innocente
summary: The prioress tells Fauchelevent that Mother Crucifixion, a saint who slept twenty years in her coffin, has died asking to be buried in that coffin under the chapel altar, which the law forbids; the chapter has agreed, and Fauchelevent must raise the vault slab that night with his lever and four mothers. He promises to deal with the empty official coffin by filling it with earth, and she tells him to bring his brother and the child after the burial.
details: After a quarter of an hour the prioress returns and the dialogue proceeds, which Hugo reports as if stenographically. There is a stone to be raised: the slab beside the altar that closes the vault, which swings on a pivot and has a ring. Fauchelevent will put his bar through it; Mother Ascension, 'as strong as a man,' and the four Mother Precentors will help him, and something must be lowered into the vault before it is closed. Then she tells him that a mother died at daybreak: Mother Crucifixion, a blessed woman who converted a Jansenist by being seen at prayer, who kept her consciousness to the last, spoke to the angels and gave her last commands. Fauchelevent, who pretended not to have heard the knell, keeps answering 'Amen' whenever Latin or piety flows, and an exchange about 'more often' tangles them both until the nine o'clock bell cuts it short.

'What the dead wish must be done.' Mother Crucifixion slept in her coffin for twenty years by permission of Pius VII and wishes to be buried in it, beneath the altar where she prayed, not in profane earth. Fauchelevent is to nail up that coffin, reject the undertaker's, and lower it into the vault between eleven and midnight in total secrecy, bell removed, with only the Precentors and Mother Ascension present; the sister at the post will not turn round. To each of his objections, the sanitary agent, the commissary, the inspector, she replies with a saint or a council: 'Forbidden by men, enjoined by God.' Fauchelevent, who has heard too much Latin, says 'Amen,' and she, whose silence has been dammed too long, pours out a torrent on Saint Bernard, Saint Benoît, the rights of the monastery over its dead, and the impiety of an age in which burial is a civil matter and God is subordinated to the commissary of police.

Fauchelevent agrees to everything, seizing every chance to mention his strong brother, 'a perfect Turk.' Then the prioress raises the last point: the empty coffin that the administration will send and the undertaker's men will carry to Vaugirard. The bearers will feel there is nothing in it. Fauchelevent nearly swears, catches himself under her sign of the cross, and improvises: he will put earth in it to give the effect of a corpse. 'Earth, that is the same thing as man,' she says, satisfied. As he reaches the door she adds gently that she is pleased with him, and that he is to bring his brother tomorrow, after the burial, and tell him to fetch his daughter.

title: In Which Jean Valjean Has Quite the Air of Having Read Austin Castillejo
summary: Fauchelevent reports that the prioress will admit 'his brother' and 'niece' tomorrow, but Valjean must somehow be outside first, and the empty coffin is a problem. Valjean solves both at once: he will be nailed into the official coffin and carried to the Vaugirard cemetery, where Fauchelevent will get the drunken gravedigger Mestienne out of the way and dig him up.
details: Fauchelevent returns to find Valjean telling Cosette that the good man will carry her out on his back in the basket, that she will wait at a lady's house and he will fetch her, and that she must obey and say nothing unless she wants Madame Thénardier to get her again. Cosette nods gravely. 'Everything is arranged, and nothing is,' says Fauchelevent: he has permission to bring Valjean in, but first he must be got out, and 'Get out as you came in' meets the same 'Impossible.' He is also troubled that earth in the coffin will shift and the bearers will notice.

He explains the bargain: the dead nun asked to be buried in her own coffin under the altar, the prioress and vocal mothers mean to do it despite the police regulations, and in return the brother becomes gardener and the niece a pupil; the brother is M. Madeleine and the niece is Cosette, to be brought tomorrow evening after the counterfeit interment. But he cannot bring Valjean in from outside if he is not outside, and the administration's empty coffin must go to the cemetery with something in it. 'Put something in it,' says Valjean. 'A corpse? I have none.' 'A living person.' 'What person?' 'Me!' Fauchelevent springs up as if a bomb had burst under his chair. Valjean smiles: Mother Crucifixion is dead, and Father Madeleine is buried; the basket he asked for will be of pine and the cover a cloth, white, since nuns are buried in white.

Valjean questions him precisely: the empty coffin stands on trestles under the pall in the ground-floor dead-room, which has a grated window on the garden and two doors, one to the convent, whose key Fauchelevent holds, and one to the public church, whose key the porter holds and opens only for the undertaker's men around three the next afternoon. Fauchelevent alone nails the coffin and spreads the pall. He can hide Valjean in the locked tool-closet opening off the dead-room overnight, bring him food, and nail him in at two o'clock, boring gimlet holes around his mouth and fixing the top plank loosely. A man making his escape, Valjean says, does not cough or sneeze. Hugo notes that such endurance in a box is one of Valjean's gloomy convict talents, and that according to the monk Austin Castillejo it was also the device of Charles V.

Fauchelevent, hesitating like a cat in a half-open door, yields to Valjean's coolness. Only the cemetery worries Valjean; that, says Fauchelevent, is the easy part. The gravedigger, Father Mestienne, is his friend and a drunkard. After the priest's prayers the two will be alone; if Mestienne is sober Fauchelevent will take him to drink at the Bon Coing, get him under the table, take his card to re-enter the cemetery and come back alone; if he is already drunk he will send him off and do his work. Then he will dig Valjean out. They shake hands: 'All will go well.' 'Provided nothing goes wrong,' thinks Fauchelevent.

title: It Is Not Necessary to Be Drunk in Order to Be Immortal
summary: The next afternoon the hearse carrying the coffin enters the Vaugirard cemetery with Fauchelevent limping behind, tools in his pocket. Everything has gone smoothly, until a stranger joins him at the gate and announces that he is the gravedigger: Father Mestienne is dead, and his successor, Gribier, a failed student and public writer with seven children, never drinks.
details: As the sun declines, passers-by on the Boulevard du Maine doff their hats to an old-fashioned hearse bearing a coffin under a white pall with a black cross, followed by a mourning-coach with a priest and choir boy, two undertaker's men, and a limping old labourer from whose pocket protrude a hammer, a cold chisel and pincers. Hugo describes the Vaugirard cemetery, a faded, old-fashioned enclosure soon to be suppressed, with its carriage gate and foot gate beside the porter's pavilion. Its gates close at sundown; a gravedigger caught inside after that can get out only by dropping his card into the porter's box, or by naming himself and paying a fifteen-franc fine. Next door stands the dram-shop Au Bon Coing.

The interment of Mother Crucifixion under the altar, the exit of Cosette and the installing of Valjean in the dead-room have all gone off without a hitch; Hugo remarks in passing that he finds the nuns' offence a venial one, a fault that resembles a duty.
