Fauchelevent follows in high contentment, sure of Mestienne, whom he has made drunk ten times in two years; he rubs his hands and says, 'Here's a fine farce!'

At the gate, while the permit is shown, a tall, thin, livid man with a mattock under his arm places himself beside him and, asked who he is, replies, 'The gravedigger.' Father Mestienne is the gravedigger, protests Fauchelevent. 'He was. He is dead.' 'After Napoleon, Louis XVIII. After Mestienne, Gribier.' Fauchelevent laughs it off and invites him to drink; Gribier announces that he has been a student, passed his fourth examination, and never drinks. As the hearse rolls up the alley Fauchelevent tries again and again: Gribier has seven small children who must eat, so he cannot drink; 'their hunger is the enemy of my thirst.' He is a public writer with a stall in the Rue de Sèvres who writes love letters in the morning and digs graves at night, and 'business first.' Fauchelevent thinks, 'I am lost.' The hearse turns into the thicket of the nuns' corner and halts with a wheel on a heap of earth beside an open grave. 'What a farce this is!' he repeats, in consternation.

title: Between Four Planks
summary: Inside the coffin, Jean Valjean follows the journey with complete composure, hears himself lowered into the grave and the Latin prayers said over him, and waits for Fauchelevent to take Mestienne off to drink. Then shovelfuls of earth begin to fall on the lid, one of his air holes is stopped, and he loses consciousness.
details: Who is in the coffin? Jean Valjean, who has arranged things so that he can almost breathe. Hugo observes how security of conscience gives security of everything else: like Fauchelevent, Valjean counts on Father Mestienne, and never was a situation more critical nor a composure more complete. Something of the repose of the dead seems to enter him between the four planks.

He has followed every phase: the nailing of the top plank, being carried out and driven off, the change from pavement to earth road, the dull sound of the Pont d'Austerlitz, the first halt at the cemetery gate and the second at the grave. He feels hands seize the coffin, the rasp of the rope, then a giddiness as the coffin tilts head-first before coming to rest horizontal at the bottom. A cold sensation follows. A glacial, solemn voice pronounces Latin over him, slowly enough for him to catch the words, and a child's voice answers; a patter like raindrops on the lid is the holy water. He thinks: soon the priest will leave, Fauchelevent will take Mestienne to drink, and within an hour he will be out.

He hears 'Requiescat in pace,' 'Amen,' and retreating footsteps. 'I am alone,' he thinks. Then a sound like a clap of thunder over his head: a shovelful of earth on the coffin. A second falls. One of the holes through which he breathes is stopped up. A third, a fourth. There are things too strong for the strongest man; Jean Valjean loses consciousness.

title: In Which Will Be Found the Origin of the Saying: Don’t Lose the Card
summary: Above ground, Fauchelevent fails to lure Gribier away from his shovel until he spots the gravedigger's card in his gaping pocket, steals it, and sends him running home to fetch it before the gates close. Alone, he opens the coffin, finds Valjean pale and still, and despairs, until Valjean's eyes open. They bury the empty coffin, leave with the card, and Fauchelevent returns Gribier's tools to his garret.
details: When the priest and choir boy have gone, Gribier takes up his shovel. Fauchelevent plants himself between him and the grave and declares, 'I am the one to pay!' for the Argenteuil wine at the Bon Coing. 'Go to the devil,' says Gribier, and throws in a shovelful; the coffin gives back a hollow sound and Fauchelevent nearly falls into the grave. He clutches the man's arm, offering to help him work by night if they first go and drink, and wonders even then whether the man would get drunk. Gribier consents to drink 'after work, never before,' calls him a bell-ringer, and throws in a second and third shovelful, saying the corpse would shriek after them if planted without a coverlet.

As Gribier bends to load his shovel his waistcoat pocket gapes and Fauchelevent sees something white at the bottom. An idea flashes through the Picard peasant's eyes: he slips his hand in from behind and takes it. After the fourth shovelful he asks calmly, 'By the way, you new man, have you your card?' The sun is touching the dome of the Invalides and the gate will close in five minutes. Gribier searches every pocket in vain. 'Fifteen francs fine,' says Fauchelevent, and turns green with him, then gives friendly advice: run home to 87 Rue de Vaugirard, a quarter of an hour away, fetch the card, and the porter will let you back in to bury your corpse; 'I'll watch it for you, so that it shall not run away.' Gribier, overwhelmed with gratitude, runs off.

Fauchelevent leans over the grave and calls, 'Father Madeleine!' No reply. He tumbles in, pries up the lid with chisel and hammer, and sees Valjean's face pale, eyes closed. 'He is dead! And this is the way I save his life!' He sobs and rails at Mestienne for dying, at himself, and at the good man who put himself under the cart, wondering what will become of the little girl and the fruit-seller. The cemetery gate grates shut in the distance. He bends over again and recoils: Valjean's eyes are open and looking at him. 'I fell asleep,' says Valjean, sitting up. He had merely fainted, and the fresh air revived him. A mouthful of brandy from Fauchelevent's gourd finishes the cure. Valjean climbs out, helps nail the lid back on, and together they fill the grave over the empty coffin.

With the gravedigger's card Fauchelevent opens the gate, and shovel and pick serve as passports at the Vaugirard barrier. At No. 87 he climbs to the garret and finds Gribier's wretched household turned upside down by a furious search for the card, the wife in tears, the children probably beaten. He lays down the shovel and mattock and says that Gribier dropped his card, that he found it, buried the corpse, filled the grave and did his work, and that the porter will return the card in the morning, so there is no fine to pay. 'Thanks, villager!' cries Gribier, radiant. 'The next time I will pay for the drinks.'

title: A Successful Interrogatory
summary: An hour later Fauchelevent, Valjean and Cosette, fetched from the fruit-seller's, present themselves at 62 Rue Petit-Picpus. The prioress questions the 'brother,' Fauchelevent answering for him as Ultime Fauchelevent, gardener from Picquigny, aged fifty, grandfather of the child; judging that Cosette 'will grow up ugly,' she admits the girl as a charity pupil and orders a second bell for the new gardener.
details: In the dark of night two men and a child knock at No. 62: Fauchelevent, Jean Valjean and Cosette, whom the old men have fetched from the deaf fruit-seller's in the Rue du Chemin-Vert. Cosette has spent the twenty-four hours trembling and silent, neither eating nor sleeping, answering the fruit-seller's hundred questions with the same melancholy gaze; she has understood that she must 'be good' and say nothing, and no one keeps a secret like a child. When she sees Valjean again she gives a cry of joy that seems to issue from an abyss. Fauchelevent knows the passwords, so all the doors open, and the porter admits them through the little servants' door into the garden and on to the reserved parlour.

The prioress, rosary in hand, waits with a veiled vocal mother beside her, and examines Valjean with downcast eyes. 'You are the brother?' Fauchelevent answers every question for him: his name is Ultime Fauchelevent (a real dead brother's name), from Picquigny near Amiens, fifty years old, a gardener, a good Christian since 'everyone is in the family,' and the little girl's grandfather. 'He answers well,' whispers the vocal mother. Valjean has not said a word. The prioress looks attentively at Cosette and says half aloud, 'She will grow up ugly.' After a whispered consultation she tells Father Fauvent to get another kneecap with a bell, since two will now be required.

Next day two bells sound in the garden and the nuns cannot resist lifting the corner of their veils to watch two men digging side by side under the trees: 'He is an assistant gardener,' 'a brother of Father Fauvent.' Jean Valjean is officially installed under the name Ultime Fauchelevent. The decisive factor, Hugo says, was the prioress's verdict on Cosette, for plain girls are likelier to become nuns; she took a fancy to the child and gave her a place in the school as a charity pupil. Fauchelevent's triumph is triple: Valjean saved, Gribier spared a fine, and the convent able to keep Mother Crucifixion's coffin under its altar, so that there is a coffin with a body at the Petit-Picpus and one without at Vaugirard, and no one the wiser. The prioress confesses and boasts of the affair to the archbishop, who whispers it to M. de Latil, and the fame of the holy gardener 'Fauvent' reaches even a note of Pope Leo XII, though nothing of it reaches Fauchelevent in his hut, who goes on grafting and covering his melons.

title: Cloistered
summary: Cosette, now a pupil, keeps silent and misses her doll; Valjean locks away her little mourning clothes in a scented valise. The nuns call him 'the other Fauvent'; he never goes out, and Javert watches the quarter for over a month. Gardening beside Fauchelevent and seeing Cosette an hour a day, he compares this cloister with the galleys, is humbled by the nuns' expiation for others, and prays each evening outside the chapel window. Years pass and Cosette grows up.
details: Cosette holds her tongue in the convent; she naturally thinks herself Valjean's daughter, and unhappiness has trained her to silence. She settles in quickly, regretting only Catherine: 'Father, if I had known, I would have brought her away with me.' Obliged to wear the pupils' dress, she gives up the little mourning suit Valjean had put on her when she left the Thénardiers' inn; he recovers it, locks it with her stockings and shoes in a small valise full of camphor and convent aromatics, keeps the key on him, and sets the valise by his bed. 'Father, what is there in that box which smells so good?' she asks one day.

Fauchelevent is happier, has half the work, and takes three times as much snuff, since M. Madeleine pays for it. The nuns do not use the name Ultime but call Valjean 'the other Fauvent.' Had they possessed Javert's glance they would have noticed that every outside errand falls to the old lame man and never to the other, but eyes fixed on God do not spy. It is as well, for Javert watches the quarter for more than a month. The convent becomes for Valjean an island surrounded by gulfs; those four walls are his world, with enough sky to keep his serenity and enough of Cosette to keep her happy. He takes the main room of the three-room hut over his own protests, under a Vendean banknote of '93 nailed up by the previous gardener, an old Chouan. Once a pruner, he gardens every day and grafts the wild orchard trees into bearing good fruit.

Cosette may spend an hour with him daily and flies to the hut at the appointed time; comparing the melancholy sisters with his kindness, she adores him, and he watches her at recreation and picks out her laugh, for Cosette laughs now. At night he rises to look at her dormitory windows. Hugo says the convent, like Cosette, completes the Bishop's work: Valjean had begun comparing himself with men in general instead of with the Bishop, and pride was springing up; the convent stops him. He sets this second place of captivity against the first. The convicts rose at dawn, slept on two-inch mattresses in rarely heated rooms, wore red blouses, lived by numbers under the cudgel; these women rise in the night to pray on cold stone, sleep on straw in unheated cells, wear black serge that gives them fever, lose their names and never eat meat. The men had stolen, violated and murdered; the women had done nothing. Both undergo expiation, but the convicts expiate for themselves and the nuns for others, 'the most divine of human generosities.'

He remembers that he had dared to murmur, and rises at night to hear these innocents sing while the justly punished blaspheme. It strikes him as a whisper from Providence that all his efforts to escape the one place of expiation were made to gain entrance to this one, a prison too, with gratings and bars to guard angels where he had seen them guard tigers, yet more austere than the galleys. His pride vanishes; he feels his pettiness and weeps often. Everything since Montfermeil has led him back to the Bishop's injunctions, Cosette through love, the convent through humility. At twilight he can be seen kneeling in the walk by the chapel, before the window through which he looked on the night of his arrival, turned toward the sister making reparation, as if he dared not kneel directly before God. The garden, the flowers, the children and the grave women permeate him, and he reflects that two houses of God have received him at the two crises of his life, one when all doors were closed to him, the other when society again hunted him. His heart melts in gratitude, and he loves more and more. Many years pass thus; Cosette is growing up.
